45-Degree Hip Extension: Rest your hips on the pad with your ankles locked under the rollers and torso hanging forward. Lower under control then drive your hips forward to bring your body level, squeezing your glutes at the top. Most people swing up fast instead of pausing and controlling the descent.
Ab Crunch Machine: Sit tall with your chest against the pad and hands on the handles, elbows bent. Curl your torso forward by rounding your spine, then return under control without letting the weight slam back. The common error is pulling with your arms rather than curling through your abs.
Abduction Machine: Sit with the outer pads resting against your thighs and your back flat on the seat. Push your knees apart against the resistance, then let them return under control without letting the stack bang down. Leaning back and using body weight to force the movement is the usual fault.
Assisted Dip Machine: Kneel or step onto the platform and set a counterweight that supports part of your body weight, then grip the parallel bars. Lower your body until your elbows bend to around ninety degrees, then press back up to straight arms. Choosing too much assistance so the muscles barely work is the common mistake.
Assisted Pull-Up: Kneel or place a foot on the platform with a counterweight set to support part of your body weight, then take a grip on the bar above you. Pull your chest towards the bar, then lower with control back to a full hang. Shrugging the shoulders up instead of pulling with the back is a frequent error here.
Back Extension (Weighted): Set your hips on the pad with your ankles secured, torso hanging forward, and hold a plate against your chest. Lower your torso towards the floor then extend back up until your body forms a straight line. Rushing the lift with a jerky swing rather than a controlled hip drive is the usual mistake.
Bayesian Curl: Set the pulley low and stand facing away from the machine so your arm hangs behind your torso at the bottom of the stretch. Curl the handle up towards your shoulder while keeping your upper arm still and slightly behind you. Letting the elbow drift forward removes the stretch that makes this curl useful.
Belt Squat: Clip the belt around your hips, step onto the platform either side of the weight, and stand tall with feet shoulder width apart. Bend your knees and hips to squat down, keeping your torso upright, then drive back up to standing. Rounding the lower back to chase depth is the most common fault.
Bent-Over Cable Rear Delt Fly: Set two pulleys low, cross the handles to grip opposite sides, and hinge forward at the hips with a flat back. Sweep your arms out and slightly back to shoulder height, then return under control. Swinging the torso to fling the handles up is the usual mistake rather than moving purely through the shoulders.
Cable Anti-Rotation Hold (Half-Kneeling): Kneel with one knee up and one down, side-on to a cable set at chest height, and hold the handle with both hands against your sternum. Press the handle straight out and hold the position without letting your torso twist towards the machine. Allowing the hips to rotate is the fault this drill is meant to catch.
Cable Behind-the-Back Shrug: Stand facing away from a low pulley and hold the handle behind your hips with both hands, arms straight. Shrug your shoulders straight up towards your ears, then lower under control. Rolling the shoulders forward or back turns this into a different movement, so keep the path vertical.
Cable Chest Press (Standing): Stand facing away from the pulleys set at chest height, one foot forward for balance, and hold a handle in each hand at your chest. Press both handles forward until your arms are extended, then return under control. Leaning too far forward to add momentum is the usual mistake.
Cable Concentration Curl: Sit or stand with your elbow braced against the inside of your thigh and your arm extended towards a low pulley. Curl the handle up towards your shoulder, keeping the elbow pinned in place, then lower fully. Swinging the shoulder to help lift the weight defeats the point of bracing the elbow.
Cable Crossover (High to Low): Set both pulleys high, take a handle in each hand, and step forward with a slight forward lean and soft knees. Pull the handles down and together in front of your hips in a wide arc, then return slowly. Bending the elbows too much turns this into a press rather than a fly.
Cable Crunch: Kneel facing a high pulley with a rope attachment held behind your head, hips stacked over your knees. Curl your spine forward and down towards your thighs, then return without letting the weight rest. The usual error is pulling with the arms or hips instead of curling through the abs.
Cable Curl: Stand facing a low pulley, grip the handle with palms up, and keep your elbows pinned to your sides. Curl the handle up towards your shoulders, then lower it fully under control. Letting the elbows swing forward as the weight gets heavier is the most common breakdown in form.
Cable Donkey Kickback: Attach an ankle cuff to a low pulley, face the machine, and hinge forward slightly holding the frame for balance. Kick your leg back and up, squeezing the glute at the top, then return with control. Using a big swing of the lower back instead of a glute squeeze is the usual fault.
Cable Face Pull: Set the pulley to roughly head height, take an attachment with both hands, and step back so the arms are extended. Pull towards your face while flaring your elbows out wide, finishing with your hands beside your ears. Pulling too low turns this into a row rather than a face pull.
Cable Face Pull (Rope): Set a rope attachment to head height, grip one end in each hand, and step back until your arms are extended. Pull the rope apart towards your face, driving your elbows high and wide, then return slowly. Letting the elbows drop below shoulder height is the most common mistake.
Cable Face Pull (Upper Back): Set the rope to around head height and step back with arms extended, keeping a slight forward lean. Pull towards your forehead while squeezing your shoulder blades together, elbows finishing high and wide. The common fault is shrugging the shoulders up instead of drawing the blades back.
Cable Fly (Chest Height): Set both pulleys level with your chest, take a handle in each hand, and step forward with a slight bend in your elbows. Sweep your arms together in front of your chest in a hugging arc, then return to the stretch. Bending the elbows more as you go turns the fly into a press.
Cable Fly (High to Low): Set both pulleys above head height and step forward between them with elbows softly bent. Pull the handles down and together towards your hips, following a wide arc, then return under control. The common error is dropping the shoulders forward instead of keeping the arc smooth.
Cable Fly (Low to High): Set both pulleys low and step forward, taking a handle in each hand with arms out to the sides. Sweep the handles up and together above chest height in an arc, then lower with control. Shrugging the shoulders up to help the weight travel is the usual mistake.
Cable Fly (Neutral): Set both pulleys at chest height, keep a neutral grip with palms facing each other, and step forward with a slight lean. Bring your hands together in front of your chest in a wide hugging arc, then return to the stretch. Letting the elbows bend further each rep turns it into a press.
Cable Front Raise: Stand facing away from a low pulley, holding the handle in front of your thighs with a straight arm. Raise your arm forward to shoulder height, keeping it straight, then lower under control. Swinging the torso to launch the weight up is the most common fault.
Cable Hammer Curl (Rope): Stand facing a low pulley with a rope attachment, gripping the ends so your palms face each other. Curl the rope up towards your shoulders while keeping your elbows tucked in, then lower fully. Letting the elbows drift forward reduces how much the forearms and biceps actually do.
Cable High Row: Set the pulley above head height, step back, and hold the handle with arms extended in front of you. Pull the handle down and back towards your ribs, driving your elbows down and behind you, then return slowly. Leaning back to help pull is the usual mistake rather than moving the arms alone.
Cable Hip Abduction: Attach an ankle cuff to a low pulley, stand side-on, and start with the working leg crossed slightly in front of the other. Sweep the leg out to the side against the resistance, then return under control. Leaning the torso to swing the leg is the common fault instead of isolating the hip.
Cable Hip Adduction: Attach an ankle cuff to a low pulley, stand side-on with the working leg out to the side, and the pulley on the far side of your body. Sweep the leg across your body towards the midline, then return with control. Using the torso to help the leg move is the usual mistake.
Cable Iron Cross: Stand centred between two high pulleys, arms out wide holding a handle in each hand. Pull both handles down and together in front of your hips in an arc, then return to the wide starting position. Bending the elbows to press the weight down instead of tracing the arc is the common error.
Cable Kickback: Attach an ankle cuff to a low pulley, face the machine, and hinge forward slightly with a flat back for balance. Drive your leg back and up, squeezing through the glute at the top, then lower under control. Arching the lower back to gain extra range instead of squeezing the glute is the usual fault.
Cable Kickback (Triceps): Stand facing away from a low pulley with your elbow pinned high and close to your body. Extend your forearm back until your arm is straight, then return under control without dropping the elbow. Letting the elbow drop as you extend takes the tension off the triceps.
Cable Lat Pullover: Lie on a bench facing away from a high pulley, or stand facing it, holding a straight bar with arms extended overhead. Pull the bar down in an arc to your thighs, keeping a slight bend in your elbows, then return slowly. Bending the elbows more as the bar comes down turns this into a pulldown.
Cable Lateral Raise: Stand beside a low pulley with the cable crossing in front of your body, arm hanging by your opposite hip. Raise your arm out to the side to shoulder height, leading with your elbow, then lower under control. Shrugging the shoulder up towards your ear is the most common fault.
Cable Lateral Raise (Behind the Back): Stand with the cable set low behind you, crossing behind your back to your working hand. Raise your arm out to the side to shoulder height, then lower under control to feel the extra stretch at the bottom. Letting the shoulder shrug up instead of leading with the elbow is the usual error.
Cable Overhead Bicep Curl: Set the pulley high, raise your arm out to the side at shoulder height, and hold the handle with your elbow bent. Curl your hand towards your head, keeping your upper arm still, then extend back out. The common fault is dropping the elbow instead of holding it in place through the curl.
Cable Overhead Tricep Extension: Stand facing away from a low pulley with a rope held behind your head, elbows pointing forward and up. Extend your arms forward and up until they straighten, then return under control. Letting the elbows flare out to the sides takes the work away from the triceps.
Cable Pull-Through: Face away from a low pulley with a rope between your legs, feet shoulder width apart, and hinge forward at the hips. Drive your hips forward to standing, squeezing your glutes, then hinge back under control. Squatting the weight up instead of hinging through the hips is the usual mistake.
Cable Pull-Through (Glute): Face away from a low pulley with a rope between your legs and hinge forward until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings. Drive your hips forward hard to standing, pausing to squeeze the glutes at the top. The common fault is bending the knees to squat the weight rather than hinging.
Cable Pushdown (Straight Bar): Stand facing a high pulley with a straight bar attachment, elbows tucked to your sides. Push the bar down until your arms are straight, then let it rise under control without the elbows moving. Letting the elbows drift away from the body is the most common breakdown.
Cable Rear Delt Fly: Stand between two low pulleys, cross the handles to opposite hands, and hinge slightly forward. Sweep your arms out and back to shoulder height, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then return slowly. Using the back to heave the handles instead of the rear delts is the usual fault.
Cable Reverse Curl: Stand facing a low pulley, take an overhand grip with palms facing down, and keep your elbows tucked to your sides. Curl the handle up towards your shoulders keeping your wrists firm, then lower fully. Letting the wrists bend during the curl takes the tension off the forearms.
Cable Reverse Curl (Forearms): Stand facing a low pulley with an overhand grip, elbows pinned to your sides, focusing on the forearm burn. Curl up keeping your wrists straight and firm, then lower with control. The common fault is letting the wrists flick forward instead of staying locked.
Cable Reverse Woodchop (Kneeling): Kneel side-on to a low pulley, holding the handle with both hands near your hip. Pull the handle diagonally up and across your body to above the opposite shoulder, rotating through your torso. Using only the arms to pull, rather than rotating through the hips and torso, is the usual mistake.
Cable Reverse Wrist Curl: Rest your forearm on your thigh or a bench with your palm facing down, holding the handle loosely. Curl your wrist up towards you, then lower it fully under control. Using your whole forearm or elbow to lift the weight instead of just the wrist is the common error.
Cable Reverse-Grip Pulldown: Sit with your thighs under the pads, take an underhand grip on the bar, and start with arms extended overhead. Pull the bar down to your upper chest, driving your elbows down and back, then return slowly. Leaning back excessively to help the pull is the usual fault.
Cable Rope Hammer Curl: Stand facing a low pulley holding a rope attachment with a neutral grip, elbows tucked to your sides. Curl the rope up towards your shoulders, then lower fully under control. The common mistake is letting the elbows swing forward once the set gets harder.
Cable Rope Straight-Arm Pulldown (Single: Stand facing a high pulley with a rope attachment, gripping one end with arm extended overhead. Pull your arm down to your hip keeping it straight throughout, then return under control. Bending the elbow during the pull turns this into a pushdown rather than a pulldown.
Cable Row (Wide Grip): Sit with your feet on the platform, take a wide bar attachment, and start with arms extended and a tall spine. Pull the bar towards your torso with your elbows out wide, then extend back out under control. Rounding the back at the start of the pull is the usual fault.
Cable Shrug: Stand holding a handle attached to a low pulley in front of your hips, arms straight. Shrug your shoulders straight up towards your ears, then lower under control. Rolling the shoulders in a circle instead of moving straight up and down is the common error.
Cable Side Bend: Stand side-on to a high pulley, holding the handle with the arm nearest the machine, feet shoulder width apart. Bend sideways at the waist against the resistance, then return to upright under control. Leaning forward instead of bending purely to the side is the usual mistake.
Cable Squat (Standing): Set the pulley low in front of you and hold the handle at chest height with both hands, feet shoulder width apart. Squat down keeping your torso upright, using the cable tension to help you balance, then stand back up. Leaning back to compensate and losing tension in the cable is the common fault.
Cable Straight-Arm Pulldown: Stand facing a high pulley with a bar attachment, arms extended and a slight forward lean. Pull the bar down to your thighs keeping your arms straight, then let it rise under control. Bending the elbows during the pull turns this into a pulldown rather than a straight-arm movement.
Cable Upright Row: Stand facing a low pulley, grip the bar with hands close together, and let your arms hang straight. Pull the bar up close to your body to around chest height, leading with your elbows, then lower under control. Letting the bar drift away from your body is the usual fault.
Cable Upright Row (Traps): Stand facing a low pulley with a close grip on the bar, arms hanging in front of you. Pull the bar straight up close to your torso, focusing on shrugging through the top, then lower slowly. The common error is swinging the torso to help lift the bar.
Cable Woodchop: Stand side-on to a pulley set at chest height, holding the handle with both hands away from your body. Rotate through your hips and torso to pull the handle across your body, then return under control. Using only the arms instead of rotating through the core is the usual fault.
Cable Woodchop (Half-Kneeling): Kneel with one knee up, side-on to a pulley set at chest height, holding the handle with both hands. Rotate your torso to pull the handle across your body towards the raised knee, then return slowly. Letting the hips shift instead of rotating through the torso is the common error.
Cable Woodchop (High to Low): Stand side-on to a pulley set above your head, holding the handle with both hands out to the side. Pull the handle diagonally down and across your body towards your opposite hip, rotating through your torso. Bending the arms to pull rather than rotating the core is the usual mistake.
Cable Woodchop (Low to High): Stand side-on to a pulley set low, holding the handle with both hands near your hip. Pull the handle diagonally up and across your body above your opposite shoulder, rotating through your torso. The common fault is pulling with the arms instead of driving the rotation from the hips.
Cable Wrist Curl: Rest your forearm on your thigh or a bench with your palm facing up, holding the handle loosely at your fingertips. Curl your wrist up towards you, then lower it fully to stretch the forearm. Moving the whole forearm or elbow instead of just the wrist is the common mistake.
Cable Y-Raise (Prone): Lie face down on an incline bench with pulleys set low, arms hanging straight down holding a handle in each hand. Raise both arms diagonally overhead to form a Y shape, then lower under control. Shrugging the shoulders up towards the ears is the usual fault.
Cable Y-Raise (Standing): Stand facing the pulleys with a slight forward lean, holding a handle in each hand at your sides. Raise both arms diagonally overhead into a Y shape, then lower under control. The common mistake is shrugging the shoulders instead of leading with the arms.
Chest Press Machine (Single-Arm): Sit with your back against the pad, gripping one handle at chest height while your other hand rests on your lap or the frame. Press the handle forward until your arm is extended, then return under control. Rotating your torso to help push the handle forward is the usual fault.
Cross-Body Cable Tricep Extension: Stand side-on to a low pulley, holding the handle across your body with your elbow bent. Pull the handle up and across, extending your elbow away from your body, then return under control. Moving at the shoulder instead of isolating the elbow extension is the common mistake.
Decline Machine Press: Sit in the machine set to a decline angle, gripping the handles level with your lower chest. Press the handles forward and slightly down until your arms extend, then return under control. Not lowering the handles fully each rep is the usual fault.
Dip Machine: Step onto the platform or take a seated position depending on the machine, and select the assistance or resistance you need. Lower your body by bending your elbows to around ninety degrees, then press back up to straight arms. Letting the elbows flare out wide is the common error.
Donkey Calf Raise (Machine): Bend forward with the hip pad resting across your lower back and the balls of your feet on the platform. Rise up onto your toes as high as possible, pause, then lower until you feel a full stretch. Bouncing quickly instead of pausing at the top is the usual mistake.
Donkey Kickback (Machine): Kneel on the pad with one foot pressed flat against the lever behind you, hips square to the machine. Push your leg back and up against the pad, squeezing the glute, then return under control. Arching the lower back to force extra range is the common fault.
Face Pull: Set a cable or band to roughly head height, take an attachment with both hands, and step back with arms extended. Pull towards your face while flaring your elbows out wide, finishing beside your ears. The usual mistake is pulling too low so it turns into a row.
Face Pull (Rope): Set a rope attachment to head height and step back until your arms are fully extended in front of you. Pull the rope apart towards your face, driving your elbows up and out wide, then return under control. Letting the hands drift below the elbows is the common fault.
Face Pull (Traps): Set the attachment slightly higher than usual, step back, and start with your arms extended forward. Pull towards your forehead while shrugging slightly through the top to bias the traps, then return slowly. Pulling too low and losing the shrug is the usual mistake.
GHD Sit-Up: Lie back on the GHD bench with your hips supported at the edge and your ankles locked under the rollers. Sit up fully under control until your torso is upright, then lower back down without collapsing. Yanking yourself up with momentum instead of curling through the abs is the common fault.
Glute Ham Raise: Kneel on the pad with your ankles secured under the rollers and your torso upright to start. Lower your torso forward under control as far as you can manage, then curl back up using your hamstrings and glutes. Letting the hips sag or bending only at the hips is the usual mistake.
Glute Kickback Machine: Kneel or stand at the machine with the pad set behind your working leg, hips square and torso braced. Push your leg back and up against the pad, pausing to squeeze the glute, then return slowly. Twisting the hips to gain extra range instead of staying square is the common fault.
Glute-Ham Raise Machine: Position yourself on the machine with your ankles locked and your hips resting against the pad, torso hanging forward. Curl your torso and legs together to raise up, driving through the hamstrings and glutes, then lower under control. Using a fast kip instead of a controlled curl is the usual fault.
Hack Squat Machine: Set your shoulders under the pads and feet shoulder width apart on the platform, back flat against the support. Bend your knees and hips to lower the platform, then drive back up to standing. Letting the knees cave inward as you push is the common mistake.
Half-Kneeling Cable Row: Kneel on one knee side-on to a low pulley, holding the handle with the arm furthest from the machine. Pull the handle to your ribs, keeping your torso square, then extend back out under control. Rotating the torso to help pull the handle in is the usual fault.
Half-Kneeling Pallof Press: Kneel with one knee up, side-on to a cable set at chest height, holding the handle with both hands against your sternum. Press the handle straight out in front of you and hold, resisting any rotation, then bring it back in. Letting the torso twist towards the machine is the common error.
Hammer Strength Chest Press: Sit in the machine and grip the independent handles at chest height, feet flat on the floor. Press both handles forward together until your arms extend, then return under control. Letting one arm lead and the torso twist is the usual fault.
Hand Gripper: Hold the gripper in the palm of one hand with your fingers wrapped around the moving handle. Squeeze the handles together until they close fully, then release under control. Only partially closing the gripper rather than working the full range is the common mistake.
High Cable Curl: Stand centred between two pulleys set above shoulder height, arms out to the sides holding a handle in each hand. Curl both handles in towards your head, keeping your upper arms still, then extend back out. Dropping the elbows down during the curl is the usual fault.
High Cable Fly: Set both pulleys above head height and step forward between them with a slight forward lean. Pull the handles down and together in front of your hips, following a wide arc, then return slowly. Letting the elbows bend more each rep turns this into a press.
Hip Adduction Machine: Sit with the pads resting against the inside of your thighs and your back flat against the seat. Squeeze your legs together against the resistance, then let them return under control. Bouncing the weight instead of controlling both directions is the common fault.
Hip Extension (Cable): Attach an ankle cuff to a low pulley, stand facing the machine, and hinge forward slightly holding the frame. Drive your leg straight back and up, squeezing the glute at the top, then return under control. Arching the lower back to gain height instead of driving through the glute is the usual mistake.
Hyperextension (Back Extension): Rest your hips on the pad with your ankles locked under the rollers and your torso hanging forward. Lower under control then extend back up until your body forms a straight line, squeezing your glutes at the top. Swinging up fast instead of controlling the descent is the common fault.
Incline Cable Chest Press: Set a bench to a moderate incline between two low pulleys, lie back, and hold a handle at each shoulder. Press both handles up and forward until your arms extend, then lower under control. Setting the bench too steep turns this into more of a shoulder press.
Incline Cable Fly: Set a bench to a moderate incline with pulleys low, lie back, and hold a handle in each hand with arms out to the sides. Sweep your arms up and together above your chest in an arc, then lower under control. Bending the elbows more each rep turns the fly into a press.
Incline Machine Press: Sit in the machine set to an incline angle, gripping the handles level with your upper chest. Press the handles up and forward until your arms extend, then return under control. Flaring the elbows out wide instead of keeping them at a moderate angle is the usual fault.
Incline Smith Machine Press: Set a bench to a moderate incline under the bar, lie back, and unhook it by rotating your wrists. Lower the bar to your upper chest, then press it back up to straight arms. The fixed bar path can pull your shoulders out of position if the bench is set too steep.
Iso-Lateral Chest Press: Sit in the machine and grip the independent handles at chest height, feet flat on the floor. Press both handles forward evenly until your arms extend, then return under control. Letting one side push harder than the other is the common mistake since the arms move independently.
Iso-Lateral Front Pulldown: Sit with your thighs under the pads, grip the independent handles above you, and start with arms extended. Pull both handles down to your chest evenly, then extend back up under control. Leaning back too far to use body weight is the usual fault.
Kneeling Cable Crunch: Kneel facing a high pulley with a rope attachment held behind your head, hips stacked over your knees. Curl your spine forward and down towards your thighs, then return without letting the weight rest fully. Shifting your hips back instead of curling the spine is the common fault.
Lat Pulldown (Close Grip): Sit with your thighs under the pads and take a close, narrow grip on the handle above you. Pull the bar down to your upper chest, driving your elbows down and slightly back, then extend back up. Leaning back too far to use body weight is the usual fault.
Lat Pulldown (Neutral Grip): Sit with your thighs under the pads and take a neutral grip on the handles, palms facing each other. Pull the handles down to your upper chest, keeping your elbows close to your body, then extend back up. The common mistake is using body swing instead of pulling with the back.
Lat Pulldown (Wide Grip): Sit with your thighs under the pads and take a wide grip on the bar above you. Pull the bar down to your upper chest, driving your elbows down and out, then extend back up under control. Leaning back excessively to help the pull is the usual fault.
Lateral Raise Machine: Sit with your back against the pad and your upper arms against the moving pads, elbows slightly bent. Raise your arms out to the sides to shoulder height, then lower under control. Shrugging the shoulders up towards the ears is the common fault.
Leaning Cable Lateral Raise: Hold a fixed post with one hand and lean your body away from a low pulley, working arm hanging across your body. Raise your arm out to the side to shoulder height, leading with the elbow, then lower slowly. Straightening back up to use your torso instead of the shoulder is the usual mistake.
Leg Curl (Cable): Attach an ankle cuff to a low pulley, stand or lie facing away, and keep your hips still. Curl your heel up towards your glute against the resistance, then lower under control. Swinging the hip to generate momentum instead of isolating the hamstring is the common fault.
Leg Extension: Sit with the pad resting on the front of your shins and your back flat against the seat. Extend your legs until they are straight, then lower under control without letting the weight drop. Swinging the weight up with momentum instead of a controlled extension is the usual fault.
Leg Press: Sit with your feet flat on the platform, shoulder width apart, and your back flat against the pad. Push through the platform to extend your legs, then bend your knees to lower under control. Letting your lower back round off the pad at the bottom is the common mistake.
Leg Press (High Foot): Sit with your feet placed high on the platform, shoulder width apart, and your back flat against the pad. Push through the platform to extend your legs, then lower under control keeping your heels down. Letting the knees cave inward as you push is the usual fault.
Leg Press (Narrow Stance): Sit with your feet placed close together in the centre of the platform and your back flat against the pad. Push through the platform to extend your legs, then lower with control. Letting your knees drift together as you push is the common mistake.
Leg Press Calf Raise: Sit in the leg press with your legs almost straight and the balls of your feet on the lower edge of the platform. Press through your toes to extend your ankles, then lower until you feel a full stretch. Bouncing quickly without pausing at the top is the usual fault.
Low Cable Fly: Set both pulleys low and stand between them, holding a handle in each hand with arms out to the sides. Sweep your arms up and together in front of your chest in an arc, then lower under control. Bending the elbows more each rep turns this into a press.
Lying Cable Curl: Lie flat on your back facing a low pulley, arms extended towards the machine holding the handle. Curl the handle towards your head, keeping your elbows resting on the floor, then lower fully. Lifting the elbows off the floor to help the curl is the common mistake.
Lying Leg Curl: Lie face down on the machine with the pad resting just above your ankles and your hips flat against the bench. Curl your heels up towards your glutes, then lower under control. Lifting your hips off the pad to gain extra range is the usual fault.
Machine Chest Fly (Single-Arm): Sit with your back against the pad, gripping one arm of the machine with your elbow slightly bent. Sweep that arm across your chest, then return under control, keeping your torso still. Twisting the torso to add momentum is the common fault.
Machine Chest Press: Sit with your back against the pad and grip the handles at chest height, feet flat on the floor. Press the handles forward until your arms extend, then return under control. Letting the handles slam back into the stack instead of controlling the return is the usual mistake.
Machine Crunch: Sit with the pad against your chest or shoulders and your feet flat on the floor or footrests. Curl your torso forward against the pad, rounding your spine, then return under control. Pulling with your arms rather than curling through your abs is the common fault.
Machine Curl: Sit with your arm resting along the pad and your hand gripping the handle, elbow aligned with the machine's pivot. Curl the handle up towards your shoulder, then lower fully under control. Shrugging the shoulder to assist the lift is the usual mistake.
Machine Hip Thrust: Position yourself with the pad across your hips and your upper back supported, feet flat on the platform. Drive your hips up until your body forms a straight line, then lower under control. Hyperextending at the top instead of stopping level is the common fault.
Machine Lateral Raise: Sit with your back against the pad and your upper arms resting against the moving pads. Raise your arms out to the sides to shoulder height, then lower with control. The usual mistake is shrugging the shoulders up rather than leading with the elbows.
Machine Rear Delt Fly: Sit facing the pads with your chest against the support and arms resting on the handles in front of you. Sweep your arms out and back, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then return under control. Using the upper back to heave the weight instead of the rear delts is the common fault.
Machine Row (Chest Supported): Sit with your chest against the pad and grip the handles in front of you, arms extended. Pull the handles back towards your torso, driving your elbows behind you, then extend back out. Shrugging the shoulders up instead of pulling with the elbows is the usual mistake.
Machine Row (Hammer Strength): Sit or stand at the machine and grip the independent handles, chest supported or braced against the pad. Pull the handles towards your torso, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then extend back out. Leaning back and heaving with the torso instead of the arms is the common fault.
Machine Shoulder Press: Sit with your back against the pad and grip the handles at shoulder height. Press the handles straight up until your arms extend, then lower under control. Arching the lower back off the pad to help press the weight is the usual mistake.
Machine Shoulder Press (Front Delt Focus: Sit with your back against the pad and grip the handles set slightly forward at shoulder height. Press the handles up and slightly forward until your arms extend, then lower under control. Flaring the elbows too wide instead of pressing through the front of the shoulder is the common fault.
Machine Tricep Extension: Sit with your arm resting along the pad and your hand gripping the handle, upper arm still. Push the handle down or forward until your arm straightens, then return under control. Moving at the shoulder instead of isolating the elbow is the usual mistake.
Machine Y-Raise: Sit facing the machine with your arms resting on the handles angled diagonally in front of you. Raise both arms up and out into a Y shape, then lower under control. Shrugging the shoulders up towards the ears is the common fault.
Neck Extension (Machine): Sit with the pad resting against the back of your head and your torso braced upright. Push your head back against the pad through a controlled range, then return slowly. Jerking the head quickly instead of moving slowly through the range is the usual mistake.
Neck Flexion (Machine): Sit with the pad resting against your forehead and your torso braced upright. Push your head forward and down against the pad through a controlled range, then return slowly. Rushing the movement instead of controlling both directions is the common fault.
Neck Harness Extension: Fit the harness around your head with the weight hanging behind you, and stand or kneel with a braced torso. Extend your head back against the resistance through a controlled range, then return slowly. Rocking the whole body to help move the weight is the usual mistake.
Neck Harness Flexion: Fit the harness around your head with the weight hanging in front of you, and stand or kneel with a braced torso. Flex your head forward and down against the resistance, then return under control. The common fault is rocking the torso instead of isolating the neck.
Neck Machine Lateral Flexion: Sit with the pad resting against the side of your head and your torso braced upright. Tilt your head towards the pad against the resistance, then return slowly to the other side. Rushing through the reps instead of moving slowly in both directions is the usual mistake.
Overhead Cable Rope Extension: Stand facing away from a low pulley with a rope held behind your head, elbows pointing forward and up. Extend your arms forward and up until they straighten, then return under control. Letting the elbows flare out wide takes the tension off the triceps.
Overhead Cable Tricep Extension: Stand or kneel facing away from a low pulley, holding a handle behind your head with your elbow bent. Extend your arm up and forward until it straightens, then lower under control. Letting the elbow drift out to the side instead of staying tucked is the common fault.
Pallof Press: Stand side-on to a cable set at chest height, holding the handle with both hands against your sternum. Press the handle straight out in front of you and hold, resisting any rotation, then bring it back in. Letting the torso twist towards the machine defeats the purpose of the drill.
Pallof Press (Kneeling): Kneel upright side-on to a cable set at chest height, holding the handle with both hands against your sternum. Press the handle straight out and hold without letting your hips or torso rotate, then bring it back in. Swaying towards the machine is the usual mistake.
Pec Deck (Machine Fly): Sit with your back against the pad and your forearms resting against the moving arms in front of you. Bring your arms together in front of your chest, then return under control to feel a stretch. Leaning back into the pad to add momentum is the common fault.
Pendulum Squat: Stand under the pivoting back pad with your feet on the platform, shoulder width apart. Bend your knees and hips to squat down along the machine's arc, then drive back up to standing. Letting the knees cave inward instead of tracking the arc smoothly is the usual mistake.
Plate-Loaded Chest Press: Sit in the machine and load plates evenly on each side, gripping the handles at chest height. Press the handles forward until your arms extend, then return under control. Loading the sides unevenly and letting one arm work harder is the common fault.
Plate-Loaded Decline Press: Sit in the machine set to a decline angle, load plates evenly, and grip the handles at your lower chest. Press the handles forward and down until your arms extend, then return under control. Not lowering the handles fully each rep is the usual mistake.
Plate-Loaded High Row: Sit or stand at the machine with plates loaded evenly, gripping the handles above chest height. Pull the handles down and back towards your ribs, driving your elbows behind you, then extend back out. Leaning back to help the pull instead of driving with the elbows is the common fault.
Plate-Loaded Hip Thrust: Position your upper back against the pad with the lever resting across your hips, feet flat on the floor. Drive your hips up until your body forms a straight line, then lower under control. Hyperextending at the top instead of stopping level is the usual fault.
Plate-Loaded Incline Press: Sit in the machine set to an incline angle, load plates evenly, and grip the handles at your upper chest. Press the handles up and forward until your arms extend, then return under control. Flaring the elbows too wide instead of a moderate angle is the common mistake.
Plate-Loaded Lat Pulldown: Sit with your thighs under the pads, load plates evenly, and grip the bar above you with arms extended. Pull the bar down to your upper chest, driving your elbows down, then extend back up. Leaning back excessively to use body weight is the usual fault.
Plate-Loaded Low Row: Sit with your chest against the pad or feet braced, load plates evenly, and grip the handles with arms extended. Pull the handles towards your torso, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then extend back out. Rounding the back at the start of the pull is the common mistake.
Plate-Loaded Overhead Extension: Sit with your arms overhead gripping the handles, load plates evenly on the machine. Lower the handles behind your head by bending your elbows, then extend back up. Letting the elbows flare out wide instead of staying close to your head is the usual fault.
Plate-Loaded Preacher Curl: Sit with your arms resting over the preacher pad, load plates evenly, and grip the handle. Curl the handle up towards your shoulders, then lower fully to extend your arms. Lifting the elbows off the pad to assist the curl is the common mistake.
Plate-Loaded Rear Delt: Sit facing the pads with your chest against the support, load plates evenly, and grip the handles in front of you. Sweep your arms out and back, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then return under control. Using the upper back to heave the weight instead of the rear delts is the usual fault.
Plate-Loaded Row: Sit or stand braced at the machine, load plates evenly, and grip the handles with arms extended. Pull the handles towards your torso, driving your elbows back, then extend back out under control. Leaning back and using the torso to heave the weight is the common fault.
Plate-Loaded Shoulder Press: Sit with your back against the pad, load plates evenly, and grip the handles at shoulder height. Press the handles straight up until your arms extend, then lower under control. Arching the lower back off the pad to help press is the usual mistake.
Preacher Curl Machine: Sit with your arms resting over the preacher pad and your hands gripping the handle. Curl the handle up towards your shoulders, then lower fully to extend your arms. Letting the elbows lift off the pad as the set gets harder is the common fault.
Prone Leg Curl: Lie face down on the machine with the pad resting just above your ankles and your hips flat against the bench. Curl your heels up towards your glutes, then lower under control. Lifting the hips off the bench to gain extra range is the usual mistake.
Reverse Cable Crossover: Stand centred between two low pulleys, holding a handle in each hand with arms crossed in front of your body. Sweep your arms up and out to the sides, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then return slowly. Swinging the torso to help lift the handles is the common fault.
Reverse Grip Cable Pushdown: Stand facing a high pulley with an underhand grip on the bar, elbows tucked to your sides. Push the bar down until your arms straighten, then let it rise under control. Letting the elbows flare out to the sides is the usual mistake.
Reverse Hyperextension: Lie face down on a raised bench with your hips at the edge and legs hanging free below you. Swing your legs up until your body forms a straight line, using your glutes and hamstrings, then lower under control. Using a big swing instead of a controlled hip extension is the common fault.
Reverse Hyperextension (Glute): Lie face down on a raised bench with your hips at the edge and legs hanging free below you. Drive your legs up by squeezing your glutes until your body is level, then lower slowly. Swinging the legs with momentum instead of a controlled glute drive is the usual fault.
Reverse Pec Deck: Sit facing the pads with your chest against the support and your arms resting on the handles in front of you. Sweep your arms out and back, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then return under control. Shrugging the shoulders instead of squeezing the blades is the common fault.
Rope Pushdown: Stand facing a high pulley with a rope attachment, elbows tucked to your sides. Push the rope down and pull the ends apart as your arms straighten, then return under control. Letting the elbows drift forward as the set gets harder is the usual mistake.
Seated Cable Row: Sit with your feet on the platform, knees slightly bent, and hold the handle with arms extended and a tall spine. Pull the handle towards your torso, keeping your back upright, then extend back out under control. Rounding the back to reach further forward is the common fault.
Seated Calf Raise: Sit with the pad resting across your knees and the balls of your feet on the platform. Press through your feet to rise up onto your toes, pause, then lower for a full stretch. Bouncing through a short range instead of pausing at the top is the usual mistake.
Seated Dip Machine: Sit in the machine and grip the handles beside you, feet flat on the floor or footrest. Push the handles down until your arms straighten, then return under control. Letting the elbows flare out wide is the common fault.
Seated Leg Curl: Sit with the pad resting on top of your shins near your ankles, back flat against the seat. Curl your legs back and down against the resistance, then return under control. Lifting your hips or thighs off the seat is the usual mistake.
Seated Machine Calf Raise: Sit with the pad resting across your knees and the balls of your feet on the platform edge. Press through your feet to rise onto your toes, pause briefly, then lower for a full stretch. Rushing through short reps without pausing at the top is the common fault.
Seated Machine Row (Wide): Sit with your feet braced and grip the wide handles with arms extended in front of you. Pull the handles towards your torso, keeping your elbows out wide, then extend back out. Using momentum from leaning the torso back is the usual mistake.
Seated Rear Delt Machine: Sit facing the pads with your chest against the support and arms resting on the handles in front of you. Sweep your arms out and back, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then return under control. Using the upper back to heave the weight instead of the rear delts is the common fault.
Seated Tibialis Raise: Sit with your heels resting on a support and the front of your feet under the padded lever. Lift the front of your feet up towards your shins against the resistance, then lower under control. Using the whole leg to jerk the weight instead of moving through the ankle is the usual mistake.
Serratus Punch: Hold a light handle or cable attachment in one hand, arm extended in front of your chest. Punch your arm further forward by reaching with your shoulder blade, then return under control. Bending the elbow instead of reaching through the shoulder blade is the common fault.
Single Arm Cable Extension: Stand or kneel facing away from a low pulley, holding the handle behind your head with one arm, elbow bent. Extend your arm up until it straightens, keeping the elbow tucked, then lower under control. Letting the elbow flare out to the side is the usual mistake.
Single Leg Press: Sit with one foot flat on the centre of the platform and your back flat against the pad. Push through that leg to extend it, then bend your knee to lower under control. Letting the hip rotate or twist to help push is the common fault.
Single-Arm Cable Lateral Raise: Stand side-on to a low pulley, arm hanging across your body holding the handle. Raise your arm out to the side to shoulder height, leading with the elbow, then lower under control. Shrugging the shoulder up towards the ear is the usual mistake.
Single-Arm Cable Rear Delt Fly: Stand side-on to a low or high pulley, holding the handle across your body with one arm. Sweep your arm out and back to shoulder height, squeezing the shoulder blade, then return slowly. Swinging the torso to help move the handle is the common fault.
Single-Arm Cable Row: Sit or stand facing a pulley, holding one handle with arm extended and your torso square. Pull the handle towards your ribs, driving your elbow back, then extend out under control. Rotating the torso to help pull the handle in is the usual mistake.
Single-Arm Cable Woodchop (Standing): Stand side-on to a pulley, holding the handle with one hand away from your body. Rotate through your hips and torso to pull the handle across your body, then return under control. Bending the arm to pull instead of rotating through the core is the common fault.
Single-Arm Cable Wrist Curl: Rest your forearm on your thigh or a bench with your palm facing up, holding the handle at your fingertips. Curl your wrist up towards you, then lower it fully to stretch the forearm. Moving the elbow or forearm instead of just the wrist is the usual mistake.
Single-Arm Lat Pulldown: Sit with your thighs under the pads, grip a single handle above you, and start with your arm extended. Pull the handle down to the side of your chest, driving your elbow down, then extend back up. Leaning away from the handle to generate the pull is the common fault.
Single-Arm Overhead Cable Extension: Stand facing away from a low pulley, holding the handle overhead with one arm, elbow bent behind your head. Extend your arm up until it straightens, keeping the elbow tucked, then lower under control. Letting the elbow drift out wide is the usual mistake.
Sissy Squat Machine: Strap your shins into the machine and hold the handles for support, starting with your body upright. Lean back and bend your knees, keeping your hips extended, until you feel a stretch in your quads, then rise back up. Bending at the hips like a squat instead of leaning back at the knees is the common fault.
Smith Machine Bench Press: Lie on a bench positioned under the bar, feet flat on the floor, and unhook the bar by rotating your wrists. Lower the bar to your chest, then press it back up to straight arms. Setting the bench too far forward or back from the bar path forces an awkward pressing angle.
Smith Machine Calf Raise: Stand with the bar resting across your upper back and the balls of your feet on a block or plate. Rise up onto your toes as high as possible, pause, then lower for a full stretch. Bouncing quickly instead of pausing at the top is the usual mistake.
Smith Machine Close-Grip Press: Lie on a bench under the bar with your hands close together, and unhook it by rotating your wrists. Lower the bar to your lower chest keeping your elbows tucked in, then press back up. Letting the elbows flare out wide is the common fault.
Smith Machine Front Squat: Rack the bar across the front of your shoulders, crossing your arms or using a clean grip, and unhook it. Squat down keeping your torso upright, then drive back up to standing. Letting your elbows drop, which lets the bar roll forward, is the usual mistake.
Smith Machine Hip Thrust: Sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench and the bar resting across your hips, feet flat on the floor. Drive your hips up until your body forms a straight line, then lower under control. Hyperextending at the top instead of stopping level is the common fault.
Smith Machine Incline Press: Set a bench to a moderate incline under the bar, lie back, and unhook it by rotating your wrists. Lower the bar to your upper chest, then press back up to straight arms. Setting the bench too steep turns this into more of a shoulder press.
Smith Machine Row: Hinge forward under the bar with your knees soft and your back flat, and unhook it with both hands. Row the bar up towards your torso, driving your elbows back, then lower under control. Standing too upright and losing the hinge is the usual mistake.
Smith Machine Shrug: Stand holding the bar at hip height, arms straight, and unhook it from the rack. Shrug your shoulders straight up towards your ears, then lower under control. Rolling the shoulders instead of moving straight up and down is the common fault.
Smith Machine Squat: Rack the bar across your upper back, feet slightly forward of the bar path, and unhook it. Squat down keeping your torso upright, then drive back up to standing. Placing your feet directly under the bar instead of slightly forward fights the fixed bar path.
Standing Cable Chest Press (Single-Arm): Stand facing away from a low pulley with one foot forward, holding the handle at chest height with one arm. Press the handle forward until your arm extends, then return under control. Rotating your torso to add power instead of pressing through the chest and arm is the common fault.
Standing Calf Raise (Machine): Set your shoulders under the pads and the balls of your feet on the platform, standing upright. Rise up onto your toes as high as possible, pause, then lower for a full stretch. Bouncing through a short range instead of pausing at the top is the usual mistake.
Standing Leg Curl: Stand at the machine with the pad resting behind one ankle, hips square and torso upright. Curl your heel up towards your glute against the resistance, then lower under control. Leaning forward and using hip momentum instead of isolating the hamstring is the common fault.
Tall-Kneeling Pallof Press: Kneel upright with your hips fully extended, side-on to a cable set at chest height, holding the handle against your sternum. Press the handle straight out and hold without letting your hips sway, then bring it back in. Letting the torso rotate towards the machine is the usual mistake.
Tib Bar Raise (Machine): Sit with your heels resting on a support and the front of your feet hooked under the bar. Pull your toes up towards your shins against the resistance, then lower under control. Rushing through the reps instead of moving slowly is the common fault.
Tricep Pushdown (Bar): Stand facing a high pulley with a straight bar attachment, elbows tucked close to your sides. Push the bar down until your arms straighten, then let it rise under control. Letting the elbows drift away from your sides is the usual mistake.
Tricep Pushdown (Rope): Stand facing a high pulley with a rope attachment, elbows tucked close to your sides. Push the rope down and spread the ends apart as your arms straighten, then return under control. Letting the elbows drift away from your body is the common fault.
Triceps Extension Machine: Sit with your arm or arms resting along the pad, hand gripping the handle, upper arm still. Push the handle down or forward until your arm straightens, then return under control. Moving at the shoulder instead of isolating the elbow is the usual mistake.
V-Bar Pulldown: Sit with your thighs under the pads and grip the V-shaped handle with palms facing each other. Pull the handle down to your upper chest, driving your elbows down and back, then extend back up. Leaning back excessively to help the pull is the common fault.
Viking Press: Stand gripping the handles with a neutral grip in front of your chest, feet shoulder width apart. Press the handles straight up overhead until your arms extend, then lower under control. Leaning back excessively to help press the weight up is the usual mistake.
Wide-Grip Cable Row: Sit with your feet on the platform and take a wide bar attachment, arms extended and spine tall. Pull the bar towards your torso with your elbows out wide, then extend back out under control. Rounding the back at the start of each pull is the common fault.
